Musical artist

**Fabrizio Cristiano De André** (Italian:[[faˈbrittsjo de anˈdre]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); 18 February 1940 – 11 January 1999) was an Italian singer-songwriter and the most-prominent _[cantautore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantautore "Cantautore")_ of his time. He is also known as **Faber**, a nickname given by the friend [Paolo Villaggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Villaggio "Paolo Villaggio"), as a reference to his liking towards [Faber-Castell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faber-Castell "Faber-Castell")'s pastels and pencils, aside from the assonance with his own name,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-1) and also because he was known as _il cantautore degli emarginati_ or _il poeta degli sconfitti_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-3) His 40-year career reflects his interests in [concept albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album"), literature, poetry, political protest, and [French music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_France "Music of France").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-4) He is considered a prominent member of the [Genoese School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoese_School "Genoese School"). He sang in both [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") and in other languages such as [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoese_dialect "Genoese dialect"). Because of the success of his music in Italy and its impact on the Italian [collective memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_memory "Collective memory"), many public places such as roads, squares, and schools in Italy are named after De André.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-5)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/DeAndr%C3%A9PlaquePegli.jpg/250px-DeAndr%C3%A9PlaquePegli.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DeAndr%C3%A9PlaquePegli.jpg)

Memorial plaque on the birth house of Fabrizio De André in Pegli

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/DeAndr%C3%A9_1960.jpg/250px-DeAndr%C3%A9_1960.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DeAndr%C3%A9_1960.jpg)

De André in 1960

Fabrizio De André was born in [Pegli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegli "Pegli"), Genoa, Italy, to an upper-class family. He had a warm, deep voice,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-6) and started playing guitar at the age of 14.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-7) His father gave him some [Georges Brassens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Brassens "Georges Brassens") records, whose songs influenced the style of his first songs.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-8) Brassens also inspired De André to become a [libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarianism "Libertarianism") and a [pacifist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacifism "Pacifism"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-9) which was influential in his music and later, more-sophisticated productions.

### 1960s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1960s")]

When he was a student in February 1961, De André debuted, singing two songs in a theater in Genoa.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-10) The two songs were later recorded as his first single, "Nuvole Barocche" b/w "E fu la Notte", which was released in 1961 and was an imitation of Domenico Modugno.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-11) In his following recordings in the early 1960s, De André found a more personal style, mixing literature with traditional songs (in particular [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") ones), presenting himself as a contemporary [troubador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troubador "Troubador") and storyteller. His narrative centered on the stories of [marginalized people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_exclusion "Social exclusion") and [antiheroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antihero "Antihero"). He later recorded [protest songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_song "Protest song") such as "La Ballata del Miché" ("Mickey's Ballad"), which he co-wrote with his friend Clelia Petracchi and considered his first true song;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-12)["La Guerra di Piero"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Guerra_di_Piero "La Guerra di Piero") ("Piero's War"), an anti-war song, with music contributed by Vittorio Centenaro, and several other songs. Some of the songs were inspired by his city, Genoa, such as "La Città Vecchia" ("The Old [side of the] City"), which he co-wrote with Elvio Monti; and ["Via del Campo"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_del_Campo "Via del Campo"), with the music of [Enzo Jannacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Jannacci "Enzo Jannacci"). He also wrote two songs with his life-long friend [Paolo Villaggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Villaggio "Paolo Villaggio"), "Il Fannullone" and "Carlo Martello (Ritorna dalla Battaglia di Poitiers)" ("Charles Martel Returns from [the Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers_(732) "Battle of Poitiers (732)")"), in 1963.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-13)

In 1962, his first son [Cristiano De André](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cristiano_De_Andr%C3%A9 "Cristiano De André") was born to his first wife Enrica "Puny" Rignon, whom he married in the same year.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-14)

His first song to find commercial success was "La canzone di Marinella" ("The Song of Marinella") in 1967, thanks to a television performance by [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina_(Italian_singer) "Mina (Italian singer)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-15) Following this first success, his first album of new songs was released in 1967 with the title _[Volume 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume\_1\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Volume 1 (Fabrizio De André album)")_. The album opens with "Preghiera in Gennaio" ("Prayer in January"), which is dedicated to De André's friend [Luigi Tenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco "Luigi Tenco"), a singer-songwriter who committed suicide before the album's release during his participation in the [Sanremo Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Festival "Sanremo Festival").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-16) Despite the popularity of this festival, De André refused to participate in any song competition by principle, and rarely appeared on television. In 1966, De André's first compilation album _[Tutto Fabrizio De André](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutto\_Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9 "Tutto Fabrizio De André")_ was released.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_and_Riccardo_Mannerini.jpg/250px-Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_and_Riccardo_Mannerini.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_and_Riccardo_Mannerini.jpg)

Riccardo Mannerini and Fabrizio De André in 1968

In 1968, De André released _[Tutti morimmo a stento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutti\_morimmo\_a\_stento "Tutti morimmo a stento")_, a concept album sung in Italian, with orchestral arrangements of [Gian Piero Reverberi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gian_Piero_Reverberi "Gian Piero Reverberi")—a first for De André. The lyrics of the first song "Il Cantico dei Drogati" ("Junkies' Canticle") were co-written with poet [Riccardo Mannerini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riccardo_Mannerini?action=edit&redlink=1 "Riccardo Mannerini (page does not exist)"), one of the most significant people in De André's life.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-17) De André and Mannerini also co-wrote lyrics for the 1968 album of the band [New Trolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Trolls "New Trolls"), _[Senza orario Senza bandiera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senza\_orario\_Senza\_bandiera "Senza orario Senza bandiera")_. In 1969, it was released on the album _[Volume 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume\_3\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Volume 3 (Fabrizio De André album)")_; due to their lyrics, some of its songs were censored by the national Italian television channel but were broadcast by [Vatican Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatican_Radio "Vatican Radio").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-18)

### 1970s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1970s")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Leo_Ferr%C3%A9_e_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9.jpg/250px-Leo_Ferr%C3%A9_e_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leo_Ferr%C3%A9_e_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9.jpg)

De André with [Leo Ferré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Ferr%C3%A9 "Leo Ferré"), 1975

In 1970 the song ["Il pescatore"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_pescatore "Il pescatore") ("The Fisherman") was released. The same year, he released _[La buona novella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_buona\_novella "La buona novella")_ (The Good News), another concept album that was inspired by the life of Jesus Christ as reported mainly by the [Apocryphal gospels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocryphal_gospels "Apocryphal gospels"). The album was followed in 1971 by _[Non al denaro non all'amore né al cielo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non\_al\_denaro\_non\_all'amore\_n%C3%A9\_al\_cielo "Non al denaro non all'amore né al cielo")_ which was inspired by the [Spoon River Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoon_River_Anthology "Spoon River Anthology"), a collection of short poems from [Edgar Lee Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Lee_Masters "Edgar Lee Masters"), with the collaboration of [Nicola Piovani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Piovani "Nicola Piovani") for the music and Giuseppe Bentivoglio for the lyrics. The album's booklet contains an interview from [Fernanda Pivano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernanda_Pivano "Fernanda Pivano"), the Italian translator of Masters' works. In 1973, De André wrote the concept album _[Storia di un impiegato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storia\_di\_un\_impiegato "Storia di un impiegato")_, which is about the protests of those years, also involving Piovani and Bentivoglio. In 1974, he released the album _[Canzoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canzoni\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Canzoni (Fabrizio De André album)")_, which includes re-recordings of many old songs and new translations of songs of Brassens, [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen") (["Suzanne"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanne_(Leonard_Cohen_song) "Suzanne (Leonard Cohen song)") and ["Joan of Arc"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc_(Leonard_Cohen_song) "Joan of Arc (Leonard Cohen song)")), and [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") ("[Desolation Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desolation_Row "Desolation Row")"), thanks to the collaboration of [Francesco De Gregori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_De_Gregori "Francesco De Gregori"). In 1975, the experimental (both musically and linguistically[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-19)) album _[Volume/8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume\_8\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Volume 8 (Fabrizio De André album)")_ was a collaboration with the songwriter Francesco De Gregori, and includes a translation of a song by Leonard Cohen ("Seems so long ago, Nancy").

In 1975, De André made his concert debut at La Bussola in [Viareggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viareggio "Viareggio").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-20) Before that event, De André refused to perform live concerts because he considered himself more a songwriter than a performer.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-21) In the same period, he moved from Genoa to [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia"). In 1978, his new concept album _[Rimini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rimini\_(album) "Rimini (album)")_, which he co-wrote with singer-songwriter [Massimo Bubola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massimo_Bubola "Massimo Bubola") was released; it includes a translation of Bob Dylan's "[Romance in Durango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_in_Durango "Romance in Durango")" ("Avventura a Durango"). For the first time, he wrote a song in [Gallurese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallurese "Gallurese"), a local language related to Corsican, "Zirichiltaggia" ("Lizard Den"), inspired by the _[Ballu tundu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballu\_tundu "Ballu tundu")_, beginning to show his passion for [minority languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_language "Minority language") and music traditions.

In 1977, his daughter Ludovica Vittoria (nicknamed simply Luvi) was born to his partner [Dori Ghezzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dori_Ghezzi "Dori Ghezzi").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-22) Between December 1978 and January 1979, De André toured with the Italian [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock") band [Premiata Forneria Marconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiata_Forneria_Marconi "Premiata Forneria Marconi") (PFM), from which two live albums (_In Concerto - Arrangiamenti PFM_, vol. 1 and 2) were released. Many years later, in 2020, a video taken from that tour was discovered and published as a DVD with the title _"Fabrizio De André e PFM - Il concerto ritrovato"_.

On 27 August 1979, De André and Dori Ghezzi were kidnapped in Sardinia.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-23) They were not released until December.

### 1980s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1980s")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Remington_the_outlier.jpg/250px-Remington_the_outlier.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Remington_the_outlier.jpg)

The Outlier, depicted by Frederic Remington, was used as cover of the 1981 album with [Bubola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubola "Bubola").

Together with [Sergio Bardotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Bardotti "Sergio Bardotti") De André translated the song "[Famous Blue Raincoat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famous_Blue_Raincoat "Famous Blue Raincoat")" with the title "La Famosa Volpe Azzurra", which was performed by [Ornella Vanoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornella_Vanoni "Ornella Vanoni") on her album _Ricetta di donna_ (1980).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-24)

In 1981, De André and Massimo Bubola released the single ["Una storia sbagliata"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Una_storia_sbagliata_(single) "Una storia sbagliata (single)"), which was dedicated to [Pier Paolo Pasolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_Paolo_Pasolini "Pier Paolo Pasolini") and appeared as an opening theme to an Italian television program. Later in 1981, in July, De André released an album without a title, also known as _[L'Indiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_(album) "Fabrizio De André (album)")_ (The Indian) due to the cover reproducing the painting _The Outlier_ by [Frederic Remington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Remington "Frederic Remington"). The album is more inspired by rock music than De André's earlier ones, partly because of the collaboration in songwriting with Bubola. The arrangements were done by the American-born musician [Mark Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Harris_(composer) "Mark Harris (composer)"), who also sings ["Ave Maria"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_ti_salvet_Maria "Deus ti salvet Maria") in [Sardinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinian_language "Sardinian language"). The track "Hotel Supramonte" was inspired by the De André's kidnapping experience.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-25) In September, De André and Ghezzi produced the next Bubola's album, _Tre Rose_ (Three Roses), where they are also credited in the chorus.

In 1982, De André, who disliked traveling, went on his first and only European tour of Austria, Germany, and Switzerland.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-26) In 1982 De André made one of his very rare TV presences, singing live the songs _Fiume Sand Creek_ (Sand Creek River) and _Andrea_ on the Italian television program _Sotto le stelle_. In 1984, [Joan Baez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Baez "Joan Baez") sang "Marinella" during an Italian public television program (_Blitz_, conducted by Gianni Minà).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-27)

In 1984 the album _[Crêuza de mä](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%AAuza\_de\_m%C3%A4 "Crêuza de mä")_ was released, a collaboration with the multi-instrumentalist [Mauro Pagani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauro_Pagani "Mauro Pagani"), a former member of PFM. This album is very unusual: its music was inspired by the Mediterranean music played with instruments from many local traditions, resulting in a special kind of [world music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music") and entirely sung in [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligurian_language "Ligurian language"). [David Byrne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Byrne "David Byrne"), later talking to _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, named the album as one of the most-important releases of the decade.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-28) In 1985, De André co-wrote the song "Faccia di Cane", however unofficially, which was performed by the New Trolls at the [Sanremo Music Festival 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Music_Festival_1985 "Sanremo Music Festival 1985"), where it placed third and won the Prize of the Critic.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-29) In 1987, De André and Pagani wrote the score of the film [Topo Galileo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topo_Galileo "Topo Galileo"). In 1988 De André sung in the song _"_ Questi posti davanti al mare _"_ together with Francesco De Gregori and [Ivano Fossati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivano_Fossati "Ivano Fossati"), who also wrote the song, included in Fossati's 1988 album _La pianta del tè_. The song won the [Targa Tenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Tenco "Targa Tenco") in the Best Song category.

In 1985, De André promised his dying father to stop his abuse of alcohol[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-30) but he continued to be a heavy smoker. In 1989, De André married Dori Ghezzi.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-31) Their marriage testimony was witnessed by the actor and life-long friend [Beppe Grillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beppe_Grillo "Beppe Grillo").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-32) In the same year, Fabrizio's brother Mauro, a corporate lawyer, who also helped Fabrizio with his career, died.

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1990s")]

In 1990 De André released _[Le nuvole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_nuvole "Le nuvole")_, another collaboration with Pagani. This album also brings a flavour of social protest, especially the song "La domenica delle salme".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-33) The album was arranged by [Piero Milesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piero_Milesi "Piero Milesi"). The first half of the album (side A) is sung in Italian while the second half (side B) is sung in Sardinian, Genoese, and [Neapolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neapolitan_language "Neapolitan language"). The album is also credited to [Francesco Baccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Baccini "Francesco Baccini") for some verses of the song "Ottocento". In 1991, De André toured released the double live album _1991 Concerti_.

In these years, De André collaborated also with other duets in Italian: _Genova Blues_ with Francesco Baccini (1990), _Davvero davvero_, with Mauro Pagani (1991), _Navigare_ with [Ricky Gianco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Gianco "Ricky Gianco") (1992), _Don Raffaé_ with [Roberto Murolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Murolo "Roberto Murolo") (1992) and _La Fiera della Maddalena_ with [Max Manfredi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Manfredi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Max Manfredi (page does not exist)") (1994). De André also performed _Don Raffaé_ live with Murolo at the 'Concerto del Primo Maggio' (May Day Concert) in 1992 in Rome.

De André also collaborated with the band [Tazenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tazenda "Tazenda"), singing a song in Sardinian ("Etta Abba Chelu") and co-writing the song "Pitzinnos in sa gherra" ("Children in the War"), both of which were included on their 1992 album _Limba_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-34) He sang in [Old Occitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Occitan "Old Occitan") with the band Troubaires de Coumboscuro ("Mis Amour") in 1995.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-35) In 1994, he collaborated on the lyrics of his son Cristiano's song "Cose che dimentico". In 1993, he performed the song ["Cielito Lindo"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cielito_Lindo "Cielito Lindo") in Spanish as an opening theme for an Italian television show of the same name.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-36) In 1996, a rearranged recording of the song _Sidún_ together with Pagani and Exodus community is included in the charity album _Fatto per un mondo migliore_ ["Made for a better world"].

In 1996 he released his last album _[Anime Salve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime\_Salve "Anime Salve")_, a concept album about solitude, in collaboration with [Ivano Fossati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivano_Fossati "Ivano Fossati"). The arrangements are by Milesi. Fossati also duets with De André on two of the songs, the tile track and "Â cùmba". The first song on the album, "Prinçesa", is inspired by [the autobiography of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princesa_(book) "Princesa (book)") the transsexual [Fernanda Farias De Albuquerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernanda_Farias_De_Albuquerque "Fernanda Farias De Albuquerque").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-37) This song was awarded the [Targa Tenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Tenco "Targa Tenco") as Song of the Year.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-38) The last song of the album, "Smisurata preghiera", summarizes the work of writer [Álvaro Mutis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81lvaro_Mutis "Álvaro Mutis"); De André also released a spanish version of the song titled "Desmedida plegaria", which was included in the score of the film _[Ilona Arrives with the Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilona\_Arrives\_with\_the\_Rain "Ilona Arrives with the Rain")_. The song was awarded the Lunezia Prize.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Via_al_mare_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_03.jpg/250px-Via_al_mare_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Via_al_mare_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_03.jpg)

Via Fabrizio De André (Genoa)

Also in 1996, De André co-wrote his only novel _[Un destino ridicolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un\_destino\_ridicolo "Un destino ridicolo")_ with writer [Alessandro Gennari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Gennari?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alessandro Gennari (page does not exist)"); in 2008, this novel inspired the film _[Amore che vieni, amore che vai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amore\_che\_vieni,\_amore\_che\_vai "Amore che vieni, amore che vai")_. In 1997, he recorded a new version of "Marinella", this time as a duo with Mina, which is included in the compilation _Mi innamoravo di tutto_. During the period of 1997–1998, De André went on the longest tour of his career, playing in arenas, open spaces, and theaters. Some of the summer dates were opened by poet and songwriter [Oliviero Malaspina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliviero_Malaspina?action=edit&redlink=1 "Oliviero Malaspina (page does not exist)"), with whom he was planning a collaboration for his next studio album.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-39) This long tour had to be interrupted because of the first signs of health problems. He was subsequently diagnosed with [lung cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lung_cancer "Lung cancer").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-40)

Fabrizio De André died in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") on 11 January 1999. Two days later, a public funeral took place in the [Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta in Carignano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria_Assunta,_Genoa "Santa Maria Assunta, Genoa"), Genoa, in front of a large audience.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-41) De André was buried in the family chapel in the [Monumental Cemetery of Staglieno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monumental_Cemetery_of_Staglieno "Monumental Cemetery of Staglieno").

Musical artist

**Fabrizio Cristiano De André** (Italian:[[faˈbrittsjo de anˈdre]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); 18 February 1940 – 11 January 1999) was an Italian singer-songwriter and the most-prominent _[cantautore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantautore "Cantautore")_ of his time. He is also known as **Faber**, a nickname given by the friend [Paolo Villaggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Villaggio "Paolo Villaggio"), as a reference to his liking towards [Faber-Castell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faber-Castell "Faber-Castell")'s pastels and pencils, aside from the assonance with his own name,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-1) and also because he was known as _il cantautore degli emarginati_ or _il poeta degli sconfitti_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-3) His 40-year career reflects his interests in [concept albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album"), literature, poetry, political protest, and [French music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_France "Music of France").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-4) He is considered a prominent member of the [Genoese School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoese_School "Genoese School"). He sang in both [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") and in other languages such as [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoese_dialect "Genoese dialect"). Because of the success of his music in Italy and its impact on the Italian [collective memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_memory "Collective memory"), many public places such as roads, squares, and schools in Italy are named after De André.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-5)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/DeAndr%C3%A9PlaquePegli.jpg/250px-DeAndr%C3%A9PlaquePegli.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DeAndr%C3%A9PlaquePegli.jpg)

Memorial plaque on the birth house of Fabrizio De André in Pegli

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/DeAndr%C3%A9_1960.jpg/250px-DeAndr%C3%A9_1960.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DeAndr%C3%A9_1960.jpg)

De André in 1960

Fabrizio De André was born in [Pegli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegli "Pegli"), Genoa, Italy, to an upper-class family. He had a warm, deep voice,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-6) and started playing guitar at the age of 14.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-7) His father gave him some [Georges Brassens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Brassens "Georges Brassens") records, whose songs influenced the style of his first songs.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-8) Brassens also inspired De André to become a [libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarianism "Libertarianism") and a [pacifist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacifism "Pacifism"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-9) which was influential in his music and later, more-sophisticated productions.

### 1960s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1960s")]

When he was a student in February 1961, De André debuted, singing two songs in a theater in Genoa.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-10) The two songs were later recorded as his first single, "Nuvole Barocche" b/w "E fu la Notte", which was released in 1961 and was an imitation of Domenico Modugno.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-11) In his following recordings in the early 1960s, De André found a more personal style, mixing literature with traditional songs (in particular [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") ones), presenting himself as a contemporary [troubador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troubador "Troubador") and storyteller. His narrative centered on the stories of [marginalized people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_exclusion "Social exclusion") and [antiheroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antihero "Antihero"). He later recorded [protest songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_song "Protest song") such as "La Ballata del Miché" ("Mickey's Ballad"), which he co-wrote with his friend Clelia Petracchi and considered his first true song;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-12)["La Guerra di Piero"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Guerra_di_Piero "La Guerra di Piero") ("Piero's War"), an anti-war song, with music contributed by Vittorio Centenaro, and several other songs. Some of the songs were inspired by his city, Genoa, such as "La Città Vecchia" ("The Old [side of the] City"), which he co-wrote with Elvio Monti; and ["Via del Campo"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_del_Campo "Via del Campo"), with the music of [Enzo Jannacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Jannacci "Enzo Jannacci"). He also wrote two songs with his life-long friend [Paolo Villaggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Villaggio "Paolo Villaggio"), "Il Fannullone" and "Carlo Martello (Ritorna dalla Battaglia di Poitiers)" ("Charles Martel Returns from [the Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers_(732) "Battle of Poitiers (732)")"), in 1963.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-13)

In 1962, his first son [Cristiano De André](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cristiano_De_Andr%C3%A9 "Cristiano De André") was born to his first wife Enrica "Puny" Rignon, whom he married in the same year.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-14)

His first song to find commercial success was "La canzone di Marinella" ("The Song of Marinella") in 1967, thanks to a television performance by [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina_(Italian_singer) "Mina (Italian singer)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-15) Following this first success, his first album of new songs was released in 1967 with the title _[Volume 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume\_1\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Volume 1 (Fabrizio De André album)")_. The album opens with "Preghiera in Gennaio" ("Prayer in January"), which is dedicated to De André's friend [Luigi Tenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco "Luigi Tenco"), a singer-songwriter who committed suicide before the album's release during his participation in the [Sanremo Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Festival "Sanremo Festival").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-16) Despite the popularity of this festival, De André refused to participate in any song competition by principle, and rarely appeared on television. In 1966, De André's first compilation album _[Tutto Fabrizio De André](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutto\_Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9 "Tutto Fabrizio De André")_ was released.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_and_Riccardo_Mannerini.jpg/250px-Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_and_Riccardo_Mannerini.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_and_Riccardo_Mannerini.jpg)

Riccardo Mannerini and Fabrizio De André in 1968

In 1968, De André released _[Tutti morimmo a stento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutti\_morimmo\_a\_stento "Tutti morimmo a stento")_, a concept album sung in Italian, with orchestral arrangements of [Gian Piero Reverberi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gian_Piero_Reverberi "Gian Piero Reverberi")—a first for De André. The lyrics of the first song "Il Cantico dei Drogati" ("Junkies' Canticle") were co-written with poet [Riccardo Mannerini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riccardo_Mannerini?action=edit&redlink=1 "Riccardo Mannerini (page does not exist)"), one of the most significant people in De André's life.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-17) De André and Mannerini also co-wrote lyrics for the 1968 album of the band [New Trolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Trolls "New Trolls"), _[Senza orario Senza bandiera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senza\_orario\_Senza\_bandiera "Senza orario Senza bandiera")_. In 1969, it was released on the album _[Volume 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume\_3\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Volume 3 (Fabrizio De André album)")_; due to their lyrics, some of its songs were censored by the national Italian television channel but were broadcast by [Vatican Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatican_Radio "Vatican Radio").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-18)

### 1970s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1970s")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Leo_Ferr%C3%A9_e_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9.jpg/250px-Leo_Ferr%C3%A9_e_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leo_Ferr%C3%A9_e_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9.jpg)

De André with [Leo Ferré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Ferr%C3%A9 "Leo Ferré"), 1975

In 1970 the song ["Il pescatore"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_pescatore "Il pescatore") ("The Fisherman") was released. The same year, he released _[La buona novella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_buona\_novella "La buona novella")_ (The Good News), another concept album that was inspired by the life of Jesus Christ as reported mainly by the [Apocryphal gospels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocryphal_gospels "Apocryphal gospels"). The album was followed in 1971 by _[Non al denaro non all'amore né al cielo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non\_al\_denaro\_non\_all'amore\_n%C3%A9\_al\_cielo "Non al denaro non all'amore né al cielo")_ which was inspired by the [Spoon River Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoon_River_Anthology "Spoon River Anthology"), a collection of short poems from [Edgar Lee Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Lee_Masters "Edgar Lee Masters"), with the collaboration of [Nicola Piovani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Piovani "Nicola Piovani") for the music and Giuseppe Bentivoglio for the lyrics. The album's booklet contains an interview from [Fernanda Pivano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernanda_Pivano "Fernanda Pivano"), the Italian translator of Masters' works. In 1973, De André wrote the concept album _[Storia di un impiegato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storia\_di\_un\_impiegato "Storia di un impiegato")_, which is about the protests of those years, also involving Piovani and Bentivoglio. In 1974, he released the album _[Canzoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canzoni\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Canzoni (Fabrizio De André album)")_, which includes re-recordings of many old songs and new translations of songs of Brassens, [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen") (["Suzanne"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanne_(Leonard_Cohen_song) "Suzanne (Leonard Cohen song)") and ["Joan of Arc"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc_(Leonard_Cohen_song) "Joan of Arc (Leonard Cohen song)")), and [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") ("[Desolation Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desolation_Row "Desolation Row")"), thanks to the collaboration of [Francesco De Gregori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_De_Gregori "Francesco De Gregori"). In 1975, the experimental (both musically and linguistically[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-19)) album _[Volume/8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume\_8\_(Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_album) "Volume 8 (Fabrizio De André album)")_ was a collaboration with the songwriter Francesco De Gregori, and includes a translation of a song by Leonard Cohen ("Seems so long ago, Nancy").

In 1975, De André made his concert debut at La Bussola in [Viareggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viareggio "Viareggio").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-20) Before that event, De André refused to perform live concerts because he considered himself more a songwriter than a performer.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-21) In the same period, he moved from Genoa to [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia"). In 1978, his new concept album _[Rimini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rimini\_(album) "Rimini (album)")_, which he co-wrote with singer-songwriter [Massimo Bubola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massimo_Bubola "Massimo Bubola") was released; it includes a translation of Bob Dylan's "[Romance in Durango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_in_Durango "Romance in Durango")" ("Avventura a Durango"). For the first time, he wrote a song in [Gallurese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallurese "Gallurese"), a local language related to Corsican, "Zirichiltaggia" ("Lizard Den"), inspired by the _[Ballu tundu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballu\_tundu "Ballu tundu")_, beginning to show his passion for [minority languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_language "Minority language") and music traditions.

In 1977, his daughter Ludovica Vittoria (nicknamed simply Luvi) was born to his partner [Dori Ghezzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dori_Ghezzi "Dori Ghezzi").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-22) Between December 1978 and January 1979, De André toured with the Italian [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock") band [Premiata Forneria Marconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiata_Forneria_Marconi "Premiata Forneria Marconi") (PFM), from which two live albums (_In Concerto - Arrangiamenti PFM_, vol. 1 and 2) were released. Many years later, in 2020, a video taken from that tour was discovered and published as a DVD with the title _"Fabrizio De André e PFM - Il concerto ritrovato"_.

On 27 August 1979, De André and Dori Ghezzi were kidnapped in Sardinia.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-23) They were not released until December.

### 1980s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1980s")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Remington_the_outlier.jpg/250px-Remington_the_outlier.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Remington_the_outlier.jpg)

The Outlier, depicted by Frederic Remington, was used as cover of the 1981 album with [Bubola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubola "Bubola").

Together with [Sergio Bardotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Bardotti "Sergio Bardotti") De André translated the song "[Famous Blue Raincoat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famous_Blue_Raincoat "Famous Blue Raincoat")" with the title "La Famosa Volpe Azzurra", which was performed by [Ornella Vanoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornella_Vanoni "Ornella Vanoni") on her album _Ricetta di donna_ (1980).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-24)

In 1981, De André and Massimo Bubola released the single ["Una storia sbagliata"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Una_storia_sbagliata_(single) "Una storia sbagliata (single)"), which was dedicated to [Pier Paolo Pasolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_Paolo_Pasolini "Pier Paolo Pasolini") and appeared as an opening theme to an Italian television program. Later in 1981, in July, De André released an album without a title, also known as _[L'Indiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio\_De\_Andr%C3%A9\_(album) "Fabrizio De André (album)")_ (The Indian) due to the cover reproducing the painting _The Outlier_ by [Frederic Remington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Remington "Frederic Remington"). The album is more inspired by rock music than De André's earlier ones, partly because of the collaboration in songwriting with Bubola. The arrangements were done by the American-born musician [Mark Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Harris_(composer) "Mark Harris (composer)"), who also sings ["Ave Maria"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_ti_salvet_Maria "Deus ti salvet Maria") in [Sardinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinian_language "Sardinian language"). The track "Hotel Supramonte" was inspired by the De André's kidnapping experience.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-25) In September, De André and Ghezzi produced the next Bubola's album, _Tre Rose_ (Three Roses), where they are also credited in the chorus.

In 1982, De André, who disliked traveling, went on his first and only European tour of Austria, Germany, and Switzerland.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-26) In 1982 De André made one of his very rare TV presences, singing live the songs _Fiume Sand Creek_ (Sand Creek River) and _Andrea_ on the Italian television program _Sotto le stelle_. In 1984, [Joan Baez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Baez "Joan Baez") sang "Marinella" during an Italian public television program (_Blitz_, conducted by Gianni Minà).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-27)

In 1984 the album _[Crêuza de mä](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%AAuza\_de\_m%C3%A4 "Crêuza de mä")_ was released, a collaboration with the multi-instrumentalist [Mauro Pagani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauro_Pagani "Mauro Pagani"), a former member of PFM. This album is very unusual: its music was inspired by the Mediterranean music played with instruments from many local traditions, resulting in a special kind of [world music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music") and entirely sung in [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligurian_language "Ligurian language"). [David Byrne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Byrne "David Byrne"), later talking to _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, named the album as one of the most-important releases of the decade.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-28) In 1985, De André co-wrote the song "Faccia di Cane", however unofficially, which was performed by the New Trolls at the [Sanremo Music Festival 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Music_Festival_1985 "Sanremo Music Festival 1985"), where it placed third and won the Prize of the Critic.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-29) In 1987, De André and Pagani wrote the score of the film [Topo Galileo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topo_Galileo "Topo Galileo"). In 1988 De André sung in the song _"_ Questi posti davanti al mare _"_ together with Francesco De Gregori and [Ivano Fossati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivano_Fossati "Ivano Fossati"), who also wrote the song, included in Fossati's 1988 album _La pianta del tè_. The song won the [Targa Tenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Tenco "Targa Tenco") in the Best Song category.

In 1985, De André promised his dying father to stop his abuse of alcohol[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-30) but he continued to be a heavy smoker. In 1989, De André married Dori Ghezzi.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-31) Their marriage testimony was witnessed by the actor and life-long friend [Beppe Grillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beppe_Grillo "Beppe Grillo").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-32) In the same year, Fabrizio's brother Mauro, a corporate lawyer, who also helped Fabrizio with his career, died.

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1990s")]

In 1990 De André released _[Le nuvole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_nuvole "Le nuvole")_, another collaboration with Pagani. This album also brings a flavour of social protest, especially the song "La domenica delle salme".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-33) The album was arranged by [Piero Milesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piero_Milesi "Piero Milesi"). The first half of the album (side A) is sung in Italian while the second half (side B) is sung in Sardinian, Genoese, and [Neapolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neapolitan_language "Neapolitan language"). The album is also credited to [Francesco Baccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Baccini "Francesco Baccini") for some verses of the song "Ottocento". In 1991, De André toured released the double live album _1991 Concerti_.

In these years, De André collaborated also with other duets in Italian: _Genova Blues_ with Francesco Baccini (1990), _Davvero davvero_, with Mauro Pagani (1991), _Navigare_ with [Ricky Gianco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Gianco "Ricky Gianco") (1992), _Don Raffaé_ with [Roberto Murolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Murolo "Roberto Murolo") (1992) and _La Fiera della Maddalena_ with [Max Manfredi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Manfredi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Max Manfredi (page does not exist)") (1994). De André also performed _Don Raffaé_ live with Murolo at the 'Concerto del Primo Maggio' (May Day Concert) in 1992 in Rome.

De André also collaborated with the band [Tazenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tazenda "Tazenda"), singing a song in Sardinian ("Etta Abba Chelu") and co-writing the song "Pitzinnos in sa gherra" ("Children in the War"), both of which were included on their 1992 album _Limba_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-34) He sang in [Old Occitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Occitan "Old Occitan") with the band Troubaires de Coumboscuro ("Mis Amour") in 1995.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-35) In 1994, he collaborated on the lyrics of his son Cristiano's song "Cose che dimentico". In 1993, he performed the song ["Cielito Lindo"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cielito_Lindo "Cielito Lindo") in Spanish as an opening theme for an Italian television show of the same name.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-36) In 1996, a rearranged recording of the song _Sidún_ together with Pagani and Exodus community is included in the charity album _Fatto per un mondo migliore_ ["Made for a better world"].

In 1996 he released his last album _[Anime Salve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime\_Salve "Anime Salve")_, a concept album about solitude, in collaboration with [Ivano Fossati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivano_Fossati "Ivano Fossati"). The arrangements are by Milesi. Fossati also duets with De André on two of the songs, the tile track and "Â cùmba". The first song on the album, "Prinçesa", is inspired by [the autobiography of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princesa_(book) "Princesa (book)") the transsexual [Fernanda Farias De Albuquerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernanda_Farias_De_Albuquerque "Fernanda Farias De Albuquerque").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-37) This song was awarded the [Targa Tenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Tenco "Targa Tenco") as Song of the Year.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-38) The last song of the album, "Smisurata preghiera", summarizes the work of writer [Álvaro Mutis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81lvaro_Mutis "Álvaro Mutis"); De André also released a spanish version of the song titled "Desmedida plegaria", which was included in the score of the film _[Ilona Arrives with the Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilona\_Arrives\_with\_the\_Rain "Ilona Arrives with the Rain")_. The song was awarded the Lunezia Prize.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Via_al_mare_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_03.jpg/250px-Via_al_mare_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Via_al_mare_Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9_03.jpg)

Via Fabrizio De André (Genoa)

Also in 1996, De André co-wrote his only novel _[Un destino ridicolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un\_destino\_ridicolo "Un destino ridicolo")_ with writer [Alessandro Gennari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Gennari?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alessandro Gennari (page does not exist)"); in 2008, this novel inspired the film _[Amore che vieni, amore che vai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amore\_che\_vieni,\_amore\_che\_vai "Amore che vieni, amore che vai")_. In 1997, he recorded a new version of "Marinella", this time as a duo with Mina, which is included in the compilation _Mi innamoravo di tutto_. During the period of 1997–1998, De André went on the longest tour of his career, playing in arenas, open spaces, and theaters. Some of the summer dates were opened by poet and songwriter [Oliviero Malaspina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliviero_Malaspina?action=edit&redlink=1 "Oliviero Malaspina (page does not exist)"), with whom he was planning a collaboration for his next studio album.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-39) This long tour had to be interrupted because of the first signs of health problems. He was subsequently diagnosed with [lung cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lung_cancer "Lung cancer").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-40)

Fabrizio De André died in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") on 11 January 1999. Two days later, a public funeral took place in the [Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta in Carignano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria_Assunta,_Genoa "Santa Maria Assunta, Genoa"), Genoa, in front of a large audience.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9#cite_note-41) De André was buried in the family chapel in the [Monumental Cemetery of Staglieno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monumental_Cemetery_of_Staglieno "Monumental Cemetery of Staglieno").
